summary: After the most aggressive monetary tightening in four decades, economists and central bankers are reviewing the causes of the cost-of-living crisis around three debates: inflation-target flexibility, the role of quantitative easing, and monetary-fiscal coordination. A Bloomberg survey of economists finds central banks will tolerate slower returns to target, use QE more sparingly, and face fiscal policy that may work against them. The piece also covers QE's costs, such as the BOE's estimated £200 billion bill, and its market distortions.
one_line: Bloomberg survey finds economists expect central banks to be more flexible on inflation targets, use QE more sparingly, and contend with fiscal policy that may counter them.
key_facts: The article says central banks have just completed the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades.
Three debates dominate the rethink: flexibility in reaching inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases, and monetary and fiscal coordination.

Bloomberg's special survey covered economists following 16 of the world's most important central banks; they expect policymakers to allow more time to return inflation to target if it means less economic damage.

Olivier Blanchard, a former IMF chief economist, and former ECB Vice President Vitor Constancio favor raising the inflation target, but it is controversial and only possible from a position of credibility.
Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said: "It would be a mistake of the first order to think you can change a goal you have set if you can't achieve it."
Gita Gopinath, the IMF's No. 2 official, says policymakers shouldn't assume that looking through supply shocks is optimal and should be ready to react preemptively.

Only 40% of surveyed economists predict central banks will use QE the same way as before; a quarter expect more sparing use, about 30% see its only role as addressing financial-stability concerns, and a small minority see no future use.
The Bank of England secured taxpayer indemnity for QE losses and estimates its purchases will cost the government over £200 billion ($243 billion) over the next decade.
The Fed experienced market turbulence when it tried to shrink bond holdings between 2017 and 2019; more recent portfolio reductions have gone fairly smoothly.

The ECB faces an extra legal burden on bond holdings because it operates in a currency union of 20 countries, and has landed in court several times over concerns about illegally financing governments and debt mutualization.
Some see the Silicon Valley Bank blow-up as a result of central bank reserves creation under QE, along with regulatory and supervision failures.

Fed Chair Jerome Powell said the Fed's assignment is to deliver price stability 'kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy,' while ECB President Christine Lagarde said hand-in-hand cooperation has proved helpful at times.
Agustin Carstens, general manager of the BIS, said growth needs to depend less on fiscal and monetary policy and more on structural policies.
Bloomberg Economics' Tom Orlik argues the time to debate a higher inflation target is after inflation is back at target, not before.
